# 2007 NFC Championship Game
The **2007 NFC Championship Game** was a National Football League (NFL) postseason game played on January 20, 2008, to determine the National Football Conference (NFC) champion for the 2007 NFL season. The contest featured the visiting New York Giants, the NFC's fifth seed, facing the second-seeded Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin . In a game characterized by sub-zero temperatures and dramatic momentum shifts, the Giants defeated the Packers 23–20 in overtime . The victory secured the Giants' berth in Super Bowl XLII, where they would go on to defeat the undefeated New England Patriots in one of the most significant upsets in league history .

The game is historically notable for several reasons, primarily the extreme weather conditions. With a kickoff temperature of −1 °F (−18 °C) and a wind chill of −23 °F (−31 °C), it stands as the second-coldest game in the history of Lambeau Field, trailing only the 1967 "Ice Bowl" . The harsh elements profoundly influenced the gameplay, affecting ball security, kicking mechanics, and player endurance. The image of Giants head coach Tom Coughlin, his face flushed red from the freezing wind, became an enduring symbol of the match, which NFL Films and media outlets have subsequently dubbed "The Chilling Championship" .

Beyond the weather, the game marked a pivotal transition in NFL history involving Green Bay quarterback Brett Favre. It served as Favre's final appearance for the Packers, the franchise with which he had spent 16 seasons, won three MVP awards, and captured Super Bowl XXXI . His final pass attempt as a Packer was an interception in overtime, which set up the Giants' winning drive . Conversely, the game is viewed as a defining moment for Giants quarterback Eli Manning, who orchestrated his third consecutive road playoff victory, dispelling criticisms regarding his consistency and leadership .

The game was broadcast in the United States by the Fox network and was watched by approximately 53.9 million viewers, making it one of the most-watched television programs in American history at the time, surpassing viewership for major cultural events and previous playoff contests .

## Background
The 2007 NFL season was defined by the New England Patriots' pursuit of a perfect season, but in the NFC, the narrative centered on the resurgence of the Green Bay Packers and the improbable, resilience-testing journey of the New York Giants. The two teams took divergent paths to the title game, with Green Bay dominating their division and New York battling through a volatile regular season to qualify as a Wild Card.

### Green Bay Packers Season
The Green Bay Packers finished the 2007 regular season with a record of 13–3, earning the NFC North division title and the number two seed in the conference playoffs . Under the direction of head coach Mike McCarthy, the team rebounded from an 8–8 campaign in 2006\. The offense was led by 38-year-old quarterback Brett Favre, who experienced a renaissance season. Favre was selected to the Pro Bowl and named a second-team All-Pro, revitalizing an offense that featured a potent passing attack with wide receivers Donald Driver and Greg Jennings .

Defensively, the Packers were anchored by defensive end Aaron Kampman and cornerback Al Harris, both of whom received Pro Bowl or All-Pro recognition . The team secured a first-round bye in the playoffs, allowing them to rest before hosting the Seattle Seahawks in the Divisional Round.

In the Divisional Round, played on January 12, 2008, at Lambeau Field, the Packers faced snowy conditions in a matchup often referred to as the "Snow Globe Game." The Packers fell behind early, 14–0, but rallied emphatically to defeat Seattle 42–20.1 Running back Ryan Grant, despite fumbling twice early in the game, set a franchise playoff record with 201 rushing yards and three touchdowns. This dominant victory set the stage for Green Bay to host the NFC Championship, with the team and its fanbase anticipating a Super Bowl return for Favre.

### New York Giants Season
The New York Giants entered the 2007 season facing significant scrutiny. Head coach Tom Coughlin was widely considered to be on the "hot seat" following an 8–8 finish in 2006 and a Wild Card round exit . The team started the 2007 season poorly, losing their first two games, including a 35–13 defeat to the Green Bay Packers in Week 2 . However, the Giants rallied to win six consecutive games, eventually finishing the regular season with a 10–6 record .

Finishing second in the NFC East behind the Dallas Cowboys, the Giants entered the playoffs as the number five seed . This seeding necessitated that they play all their postseason games on the road. The team's identity was forged in Week 17 of the regular season when, despite having already clinched a playoff spot, they played their starters against the undefeated New England Patriots. Although the Giants lost 38–35, the competitive nature of the game provided the team with a confidence boost heading into the postseason .

The Giants' road to the NFC Championship was characterized by upsets over higher-seeded opponents, earning them the moniker "Road Warriors" .

* **Wild Card Round:** On January 6, 2008, the Giants traveled to Raymond James Stadium and defeated the NFC South champion Tampa Bay Buccaneers, 24–14.3 
* **Divisional Round:** On January 13, 2008, the Giants faced their division rivals and the NFC's number one seed, the Dallas Cowboys, at Texas Stadium. The Giants won 21–17, marking the first time in NFL history that an NFC number four seed or lower defeated a number one seed in the divisional round .

By defeating Dallas, the Giants extended their road winning streak to nine games and set up a rematch with the Packers .

### Series History and Matchup
The 2007 NFC Championship Game was the seventh postseason meeting between the Giants and the Packers . The rivalry between the two franchises dates back to the league's early years, featuring five NFL Championship Games played between 1938 and 1962 .

* **1938 NFL Championship:** Giants defeated Packers 23–17. 
* **1939 NFL Championship:** Packers defeated Giants 27–0. 
* **1944 NFL Championship:** Packers defeated Giants 14–7. 
* **1961 NFL Championship:** Packers defeated Giants 37–0. 
* **1962 NFL Championship:** Packers defeated Giants 16–7.

In more recent history, the Giants had defeated the Packers in the 2002 Wild Card playoffs, but the Packers had not lost a playoff game at Lambeau Field prior to the 2002 season (when they lost to the Atlanta Falcons) .

Entering the 2007 NFC Championship, the Packers were considered the favorites. Oddsmakers established Green Bay as a 7.5-point favorite . The Packers' 35–13 victory over the Giants in Week 2 of the regular season was cited as a primary reason for the confidence in Green Bay, although observers noted that the Giants had evolved significantly as a team since September .

## Pre-Game Conditions
### Weather
The weather forecast for Green Bay, Wisconsin, dominated the pre-game narrative. The National Weather Service issued a wind chill advisory for the region, predicting dangerous cold . The conditions at kickoff confirmed these fears, creating one of the most hostile environments in NFL playoff history.

* **Temperature:** −1 °F (−18 °C) . 
* **Wind Chill:** −23 °F (−31 °C) . 
* **Wind Speed:** 12 miles per hour . 
* **Conditions:** Clear skies, frozen turf .

These conditions made the game the second-coldest in the history of Lambeau Field, a stadium renowned for its "frozen tundra" lore . Only the 1967 "Ice Bowl" against the Dallas Cowboys, which featured a temperature of −13 °F (−25 °C) and a wind chill of −48 °F, was colder .

The extreme cold had tangible effects on the game and the stadium experience. Reports indicated that beer sold in the stands froze inside the bottles before it could be consumed . Hand warmers were distributed to the 72,740 fans in attendance . On the sidelines, massive heaters were used to keep players warm, but the exposure to the elements was unavoidable. Giants head coach Tom Coughlin opted not to wear a face mask or scarf, and television cameras frequently captured his face turning a deep, frostbitten red, a visual that became emblematic of the game's intensity . Giants center Shaun O'Hara later remarked, "I've never felt pain like that in my fingertips before" .

### Venue
The game was held at **Lambeau Field**, the historic home of the Green Bay Packers. The stadium's natural grass surface was frozen hard, impacting footing and the behavior of the ball when it hit the ground. The attendance was a sellout of 72,740.1

### Officiating Crew
The game was officiated by referee **Terry McAulay** and his crew .

## Game Summary
The game was a physical contest of attrition, with both teams relying heavily on field position and managing the difficult conditions. While Green Bay relied on big plays in the passing game, the Giants focused on a punishing ground attack to wear down the Packers' defense.

### First Quarter
The game began with the Packers winning the coin toss and electing to receive, looking to establish early dominance at home. However, the first quarter was defined by defensive stalemates as both teams adjusted to the frozen ball and footing.

The Giants managed to construct the first scoring drive of the game late in the quarter. Utilizing the running back tandem of Brandon Jacobs and Ahmad Bradshaw, New York moved into scoring position. The drive stalled in the red zone, leading to a field goal attempt. Kicker Lawrence Tynes successfully converted a 29-yard field goal with 4:50 remaining in the first quarter, giving the Giants a 3–0 lead .

**Score at end of First Quarter:** New York Giants 3, Green Bay Packers 0 .

### Second Quarter
The second quarter saw an explosion of scoring as both offenses found a rhythm despite the cold.

The Giants extended their lead early in the period. After a drive spanning 7 plays and 38 yards, the offense was halted again by the Packers' defense. Tynes entered the game and kicked a 37-yard field goal at the 11:41 mark, extending the lead to 6–0.1

The Packers responded immediately and explosively. On the very first play of their ensuing possession, Brett Favre dropped back and launched a deep pass down the sideline to wide receiver Donald Driver. Driver caught the ball and outran the Giants' secondary for a 90-yard touchdown reception . This play stands as the longest pass play in Green Bay Packers postseason history . Mason Crosby’s extra point gave Green Bay their first lead of the game at 7–6 with 11:18 remaining in the half .

Following the touchdown, the game settled back into a defensive rhythm until the final minutes of the half. The Packers mounted another scoring drive, covering 29 yards in 8 plays. The short field, set up by field position, allowed Green Bay to add to their lead. With 1:30 remaining in the second quarter, Mason Crosby converted a 36-yard field goal, making the score 10–6.1

The Giants attempted a two-minute drill to narrow the gap before halftime. They drove 40 yards downfield, but the drive ended when the Packers' defense recorded a sack on fourth down, resulting in a turnover on downs . The Packers ran one play to exhaust the clock.

**Halftime Score:** Green Bay Packers 10, New York Giants 6 .

### Third Quarter
The Giants emerged from the halftime break with a renewed commitment to the running game. The cold weather began to fatigue the defense, and the Giants' physical offensive line began to open lanes for Jacobs and Bradshaw.

New York regained the lead on their opening possession of the second half. The drive culminated in a 1-yard touchdown run by the 264-pound running back Brandon Jacobs with 7:56 remaining in the quarter . Lawrence Tynes added the extra point, putting the Giants ahead 13–10.

The lead changed hands again quickly. Favre, displaying the improvisation that defined his career, led the Packers downfield. He capped the drive with a 12-yard touchdown pass to tight end Donald Lee with 5:00 remaining in the quarter. Crosby's extra point restored the Packers' lead at 17–13.12

Refusing to fold, the Giants responded with another touchdown drive. This time, it was the agile rookie running back Ahmad Bradshaw who finished the drive with a 4-yard touchdown run at the 2:12 mark . The successful conversion gave the Giants a 20–17 lead heading into the final quarter, setting up a dramatic finish.

**Score at end of Third Quarter:** New York Giants 20, Green Bay Packers 17 .

### Fourth Quarter
The fourth quarter was a tense affair filled with missed opportunities and special teams drama.

Early in the quarter, the Packers capitalized on a scoring opportunity to tie the game. Mason Crosby kicked a 37-yard field goal with 11:46 remaining, leveling the score at 20–20.12

For the remainder of regulation, the Giants had multiple chances to secure the victory, but special teams execution faltered in the freezing conditions.

1. **First Miss:** With 6:49 remaining in regulation, the Giants drove into field goal range. Lawrence Tynes attempted a 43-yard field goal. Tynes later admitted he misplayed the wind, which was gusting at 15 mph, and the kick hooked wide left . 
2. **Second Miss:** In the final minute of the game, Eli Manning connected with rookie wide receiver Steve Smith on passes of 15, 14, and 11 yards, moving the Giants deep into Packers territory . With just 4 seconds remaining on the clock, the Giants lined up for a game-winning 36-yard field goal. The snap from rookie long snapper Jay Alford was high, disrupting the timing of holder Jeff Feagles. Tynes managed to kick the ball, but the disruption resulted in a low "knuckleball" trajectory that hooked wide left as time expired .

Tynes was visibly distraught, having missed two potential game-winning kicks in the fourth quarter of a conference championship game. The game headed to overtime tied at 20\.

**Score at end of Regulation:** New York Giants 20, Green Bay Packers 20 .

### Overtime
The game utilized the sudden-death overtime rules in effect at the time, meaning the first team to score any points would be declared the winner. The Packers won the coin toss and elected to receive, giving Brett Favre and the offense the first opportunity to win the game .

The Packers began their drive at their own 26-yard line. On the first play, Ryan Grant rushed for a minimal gain. On the second play of overtime, Favre dropped back and looked for Donald Driver. He threw a pass intended for the receiver, but Giants cornerback Corey Webster read the play, jumped the route, and intercepted the ball . Webster returned the interception to the Green Bay 34-yard line, placing the Giants immediately in scoring range.

This interception would historically stand as Brett Favre's final pass attempt as a member of the Green Bay Packers .

The Giants took over with excellent field position. Unlike regulation, where they moved the ball aggressively, they ran three conservative plays that netted only five yards, setting up a fourth down . Despite Tynes' two previous misses, head coach Tom Coughlin sent the kicking unit onto the field for a 47-yard attempt—longer than the 43-yarder Tynes had missed earlier.

With 2:35 elapsed in overtime, Tynes approached the ball. The snap and hold were clean. Tynes struck the ball firmly, and it sailed through the uprights, good for a 47-yard field goal . Tynes immediately sprinted toward the locker room tunnel in celebration as his teammates mobbed him on the field. The Giants had won 23–20.

### Scoring Summary
The following table details the scoring plays of the game .

| Quarter | Time | Team | Scoring Play | Score (NYG-GB) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | 4:50 | NYG | FG: Lawrence Tynes 29 yards | 3–0 |
| 2 | 11:41 | NYG | FG: Lawrence Tynes 37 yards | 6–0 |
| 2 | 11:18 | GB | TD: Donald Driver 90-yard pass from Brett Favre (Mason Crosby kick) | 6–7 |
| 2 | 1:30 | GB | FG: Mason Crosby 36 yards | 6–10 |
| 3 | 7:56 | NYG | TD: Brandon Jacobs 1-yard run (Lawrence Tynes kick) | 13–10 |
| 3 | 5:00 | GB | TD: Donald Lee 12-yard pass from Brett Favre (Mason Crosby kick) | 13–17 |
| 3 | 2:12 | NYG | TD: Ahmad Bradshaw 4-yard run (Lawrence Tynes kick) | 20–17 |
| 4 | 11:46 | GB | FG: Mason Crosby 37 yards | 20–20 |
| OT | 12:25 | NYG | FG: Lawrence Tynes 47 yards | 23–20 |

## Statistical Analysis
### Team Statistics
The statistical profile of the game highlights the Giants' dominance in the running game and time of possession, which proved critical in the arctic conditions.

* **Rushing Yards:** The Giants rushed for **134 yards**, while the Packers were held to just **28 yards** on the ground . This disparity allowed New York to control the tempo and keep the Packers' offense off the field. 
* **Total Plays:** The Giants ran significantly more offensive plays than Green Bay, wearing down the Packers' defense in the extreme cold. 
* **Turnovers:** The Giants played a clean game with zero turnovers. The Packers committed two turnovers, including the fatal interception in overtime .

### Individual Performances
**New York Giants:**

* **Eli Manning:** Manning managed the game efficiently in difficult conditions, avoiding turnovers. He utilized his wide receivers, particularly Plaxico Burress, effectively to move the chains. 
* **Plaxico Burress:** Burress was a dominant force, recording **11 receptions**, which proved vital for the Giants' ball-control strategy . 
* **Brandon Jacobs & Ahmad Bradshaw:** The running back duo combined for the bulk of the Giants' 134 rushing yards and scored both of the team's touchdowns . 
* **Lawrence Tynes:** Despite missing two field goals in the fourth quarter, Tynes finished 3-for-5 on field goal attempts, including the game-winner .

**Green Bay Packers:**

* **Brett Favre:** Favre finished with a mixed performance. While he threw a 90-yard touchdown pass, he struggled to sustain drives consistently and threw the game-ending interception. 
* **Donald Driver:** Driver was the standout performer for Green Bay, catching 5 passes for **141 yards** and a touchdown . 
* **Ryan Grant:** After a record-setting performance the previous week, Grant was neutralized by the Giants' defense, gaining negligible yardage on the ground.

## Broadcasting and Media
The game was broadcast nationally in the United States on the **Fox** network. The commentary team consisted of Joe Buck providing play-by-play, Troy Aikman providing color commentary, and Pam Oliver and Chris Myers serving as sideline reporters .

### Television Ratings
The 2007 NFC Championship Game drew massive television ratings, reflecting the popularity of the two franchises and the dramatic nature of the contest.

* **Viewership:** The broadcast averaged **53.9 million viewers**.7 Other reports cite the figure at 48.6 million viewers 15, but regardless of the specific metric used, it was the most-watched television program since the series finale of the sitcom *Seinfeld* in 1998 . 
* **Ratings:** The game earned a 31.7 overnight rating and a 46 share, meaning nearly half of all televisions in use at the time were tuned to the game . 
* **Comparison:** The viewership represented a significant increase over the previous year's NFC Championship Game (43.2 million) and the AFC Championship Game played earlier the same day (Patriots vs. Chargers) .

### Cultural Impact
The game is frequently cited in NFL media as one of the most memorable playoff games of the 2000s. The visuals of the frozen breath of the players, the red face of Tom Coughlin, and the snow-hardened Lambeau Field turf have been used extensively in NFL Films productions. The game's nickname, "The Chilling Championship," reflects both the temperature and the dramatic tension of the overtime finish .

## Aftermath and Legacy
### New York Giants: Super Bowl Champions
The victory advanced the Giants to **Super Bowl XLII**, played on February 3, 2008, in Glendale, Arizona. They entered the game as heavy underdogs against the New England Patriots, who had completed a perfect 16–0 regular season and were 18–0 entering the Super Bowl.

The Giants' win over Green Bay was their 10th consecutive road victory of the season, a streak that spanned both the regular season and the playoffs . In the Super Bowl, the Giants defeated the Patriots 17–14, executing one of the biggest upsets in sports history and denying New England the first 19–0 season in NFL history . The victory over the Packers is viewed as the toughest test the Giants faced during their playoff run, proving their ability to win in hostile environments.

### Brett Favre's Departure
The aftermath of the game for the Green Bay Packers was dominated by the saga of Brett Favre.

* **Retirement:** On March 6, 2008, less than two months after the loss, Favre held an emotional press conference announcing his retirement from professional football . He cited mental fatigue and a desire to leave the game on his own terms. 
* **Un-retirement and Trade:** In the summer of 2008, Favre expressed a desire to return to the team. However, the Packers management, led by General Manager Ted Thompson and Head Coach Mike McCarthy, had committed to moving forward with quarterback Aaron Rodgers. This led to a tense standoff and Favre's eventual trade to the New York Jets in August 2008 . 
* **Legacy of the Game:** The interception thrown by Favre in overtime to Corey Webster remains the final play of his storied career in Green Bay .

### Tom Coughlin's Job Security
For Giants head coach Tom Coughlin, the victory was a vindication. Entering the season on the "hot seat," Coughlin's job status was a constant subject of media speculation. The playoff run, characterized by discipline and physical play in adverse conditions, secured his tenure with the team. He would go on to coach the Giants to another Super Bowl victory (Super Bowl XLVI) four years later, again defeating the Packers at Lambeau Field in the playoffs along the way .

### Lawrence Tynes' Redemption
Kicker Lawrence Tynes' performance in the game—missing two fourth-quarter field goals before making the winner in overtime—became a defining moment of his career. He is the only kicker in NFL history to have two postseason game-winning field goals in overtime (he kicked another one in the 2011 NFC Championship Game against the San Francisco 49ers) . His resilience in the 2007 title game is often cited by coaches and players as an example of mental toughness.

For the remainder of regulation, the Giants had multiple chances to secure the victory, but special teams execution faltered in the freezing conditions.
With 6:49 remaining in regulation, the Giants drove into field goal range.
Lawrence Tynes attempted a 43-yard field goal.
Tynes later admitted he misplayed the wind, which was gusting at 15 mph, and the kick hooked wide left.
In the final minute of the game, Eli Manning connected with rookie wide receiver Steve Smith on passes of 15, 14, and 11 yards, moving the Giants deep into Packers territory.
With just 4 seconds remaining on the clock, the Giants lined up for a game-winning 36-yard field goal.
The snap from rookie long snapper Jay Alford was high, disrupting the timing of holder Jeff Feagles.
Tynes managed to kick the ball, but the disruption resulted in a low "knuckleball" trajectory that hooked wide left as time expired.
Tynes was visibly distraught, having missed two potential game-winning kicks in the fourth quarter of a conference championship game.
The game headed to overtime tied at 20.
The score at the end of Regulation was New York Giants 20, Green Bay Packers 20.
The game utilized the sudden-death overtime rules in effect at the time, meaning the first team to score any points would be declared the winner.
The Packers won the coin toss and elected to receive, giving Brett Favre and the offense the first opportunity to win the game.
The Packers began their drive at their own 26-yard line.
On the first play, Ryan Grant rushed for a minimal gain.
On the second play of overtime, Favre dropped back and looked for Donald Driver.
Favre threw a pass intended for the receiver, but Giants cornerback Corey Webster read the play, jumped the route, and intercepted the ball.
Webster returned the interception to the Green Bay 34-yard line, placing the Giants immediately in scoring range.
This interception would historically stand as Brett Favre's final pass attempt as a member of the Green Bay Packers.
The Giants took over with excellent field position.
Unlike regulation, where they moved the ball aggressively, they ran three conservative plays that netted only five yards, setting up a fourth down.
Despite Tynes' two previous misses, head coach Tom Coughlin sent the kicking unit onto the field for a 47-yard attempt—longer than the 43-yarder Tynes had missed earlier.
With 2:35 elapsed in overtime, Tynes approached the ball.
The snap and hold were clean.
Tynes struck the ball firmly, and it sailed through the uprights, good for a 47-yard field goal.
Tynes immediately sprinted toward the locker room tunnel in celebration as his teammates mobbed him on the field.
The Giants had won 23–20.
The following table details the scoring plays of the game.
The Giants rushed for 134 yards.
The Packers were held to just 28 yards on the ground.
This disparity allowed New York to control the tempo and keep the Packers' offense off the field.
The Giants played a clean game with zero turnovers.
The Packers committed two turnovers, including the fatal interception in overtime.
Plaxico Burress was a dominant force, recording 11 receptions, which proved vital for the Giants' ball-control strategy.
The running back duo of Brandon Jacobs and Ahmad Bradshaw combined for the bulk of the Giants' 134 rushing yards and scored both of the team's touchdowns.
Despite missing two field goals in the fourth quarter, Lawrence Tynes finished 3-for-5 on field goal attempts, including the game-winner.
Donald Driver was the standout performer for Green Bay, catching 5 passes for 141 yards and a touchdown.
The game was broadcast nationally in the United States on the Fox network.
The commentary team consisted of Joe Buck providing play-by-play, Troy Aikman providing color commentary, and Pam Oliver and Chris Myers serving as sideline reporters.
The broadcast averaged 53.9 million viewers.
Other reports cite the viewership figure at 48.6 million viewers.
The game was the most-watched television program since the series finale of the sitcom Seinfeld in 1998.
The game earned a 31.7 overnight rating and a 46 share.
Nearly half of all televisions in use at the time were tuned to the game.
The viewership represented a significant increase over the previous year's NFC Championship Game (43.2 million) and the AFC Championship Game played earlier the same day (Patriots vs. Chargers).
The game is frequently cited in NFL media as one of the most memorable playoff games of the 2000s.
The visuals of the frozen breath of the players, the red face of Tom Coughlin, and the snow-hardened Lambeau Field turf have been used extensively in NFL Films productions.
The game's nickname, "The Chilling Championship," reflects both the temperature and the dramatic tension of the overtime finish.
The victory advanced the Giants to Super Bowl XLII, played on February 3, 2008, in Glendale, Arizona.
The Giants entered Super Bowl XLII as heavy underdogs against the New England Patriots.
The New England Patriots had completed a perfect 16–0 regular season and were 18–0 entering the Super Bowl.
The Giants' win over Green Bay was their 10th consecutive road victory of the season, a streak that spanned both the regular season and the playoffs.
In the Super Bowl, the Giants defeated the Patriots 17–14, executing one of the biggest upsets in sports history and denying New England the first 19–0 season in NFL history.
The victory over the Packers is viewed as the toughest test the Giants faced during their playoff run, proving their ability to win in hostile environments.
On March 6, 2008, less than two months after the loss, Favre held an emotional press conference announcing his retirement from professional football.
Brett Favre cited mental fatigue and a desire to leave the game on his own terms.
In the summer of 2008, Favre expressed a desire to return to the team.
The Packers management, led by General Manager Ted Thompson and Head Coach Mike McCarthy, had committed to moving forward with quarterback Aaron Rodgers.
This led to a tense standoff and Favre's eventual trade to the New York Jets in August 2008.
The interception thrown by Favre in overtime to Corey Webster remains the final play of his storied career in Green Bay.
For Giants head coach Tom Coughlin, the victory was a vindication.
Entering the season on the "hot seat," Coughlin's job status was a constant subject of media speculation.
The playoff run, characterized by discipline and physical play in adverse conditions, secured Tom Coughlin's tenure with the team.
Tom Coughlin would go on to coach the Giants to another Super Bowl victory (Super Bowl XLVI) four years later.
Tom Coughlin again defeated the Packers at Lambeau Field in the playoffs along the way to Super Bowl XLVI.
Kicker Lawrence Tynes' performance in the game—missing two fourth-quarter field goals before making the winner in overtime—became a defining moment of his career.
Lawrence Tynes is the only kicker in NFL history to have two postseason game-winning field goals in overtime.
Lawrence Tynes kicked another game-winning field goal in the 2011 NFC Championship Game against the San Francisco 49ers.
Lawrence Tynes' resilience in the 2007 title game is often cited by coaches and players as an example of mental toughness.

Date January 20, 2008
Stadium[Lambeau Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeau_Field "Lambeau Field")

[Green Bay, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay,_Wisconsin "Green Bay, Wisconsin"), U.S.

TV in the United States
Network[Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_on_Fox "NFL on Fox")
Announcers[Joe Buck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Buck "Joe Buck"), [Troy Aikman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_Aikman "Troy Aikman"), [Pam Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pam_Oliver "Pam Oliver"), and [Chris Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Myers "Chris Myers")

The **2007 National Football Conference (NFC) Championship Game** was an [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") game played between the [New York Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Giants "New York Giants") and the [Green Bay Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") on January 20, 2008, at [Lambeau Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeau_Field "Lambeau Field") in [Green Bay, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay,_Wisconsin "Green Bay, Wisconsin"), United States. The Packers finished the season 13–3, winning the [NFC North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFC_North "NFC North"), while securing the second seed in the playoffs. The Giants entered the playoffs as a Wild Card team, with a record of 10–6. They did not win the [NFC East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFC_East "NFC East"), which was won by the [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys"), who secured the first seed in the playoffs via a head-to-head tiebreaker with the Packers. The Giants beat the [Tampa Bay Buccaneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers "Tampa Bay Buccaneers") and the Cowboys in the Wild Card and Divisional rounds, respectively. The Packers beat the [Seattle Seahawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Seahawks "Seattle Seahawks") in the Divisional round. By virtue of their higher seeding, the Packers were given home field advantage for the Championship Game. The game was a continuation of [the two teams' rivalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giants%E2%80%93Packers_rivalry "Giants–Packers rivalry"), which included five [NFL Championship Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Championship_Game "NFL Championship Game") from the 1930s to the 1960s.

The game was marked by cold weather, with the [wind chill factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_chill_factor "Wind chill factor") bringing the temperature down to −23°F (−31°C), making it the second coldest game in Lambeau Field history. The teams went back and forth, with the Packers capitalizing on a 90-yard touchdown pass in the first half. The Giants leaned on their running attack, outgaining the Packers in rushing yards 114 to 28. Each team had mistakes: the Giants missed two field goals, including a possible game-winner at the end of the fourth quarter that led to overtime. The Packers had three turnovers, with Favre throwing an interception on the second play of overtime. The Giants won the game on a walk-off field goal by [Lawrence Tynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Tynes "Lawrence Tynes") four plays after Favre's interception, sending them to [Super Bowl XLII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLII "Super Bowl XLII"), where they would beat the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots"). The NFC Championship Game, which became part of the Giants–Packers rivalry, was notable for its competitiveness, cold weather, and impact on each team. The game helped establish [Eli Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Manning "Eli Manning")'s career, while for Favre, it became the last he would play for the Packers. He was traded during the offseason to the [New York Jets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Jets "New York Jets"), with [Aaron Rodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Rodgers "Aaron Rodgers") being named starting quarterback for the Packers.

The [New York Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Giants "New York Giants") were coming off of a Wild playoff berth in 2006 with a record of 8–8.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-1) The Giants began the season with two consecutive losses, including a 35–13 blowout loss to the [Green Bay Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") in Week 2. The Giants then won six straight games going into their bye week to bring their record to 6–2. After their bye week, they split their remaining eight games to finish with a record of 10–6.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-2) The Giants were led by a productive rushing attack behind [Brandon Jacobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Jacobs "Brandon Jacobs"), [Derrick Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derrick_Ward "Derrick Ward"), and [Reuben Droughns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuben_Droughns "Reuben Droughns"), who combined for almost 2,000 yards and 13 rushing touchdowns.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-3) Although the Giants did not win their division, as the [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") went 13–3, their record was good enough to secure the fifth seed and a Wild Card playoff berth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-PLAYOFFS-4) The Giants beat the [Tampa Bay Buccaneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers "Tampa Bay Buccaneers") in the Wild Card round by [a score of 24–8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_NFL_playoffs#NFC:_New_York_Giants_24,_Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers_14 "2007–08 NFL playoffs"), earning a match-up with the Cowboys.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-5) The Giants beat the Cowboys [21–17 in the Divisional round](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_NFL_playoffs#NFC:_New_York_Giants_21,_Dallas_Cowboys_17 "2007–08 NFL playoffs") to proceed to the NFC Championship Game.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-6)

The Packers missed the playoffs in 2006 with a record of 8–8, after losing out the playoff tiebreaker to the Giants.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-7) They finished the 2007 season with a record with of 13–3, the same as the Cowboys, which included two losses to the [Chicago Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bears "Chicago Bears").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-07PLAYOFFS-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-9) Their other loss was to the Cowboys, which ended up being the tiebreaker for the first seed in the playoffs.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-07PLAYOFFS-8) They won the [NFC North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFC_North "NFC North") division. With their head-to-head match-up loss, the Packers were given the second seed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-07PLAYOFFS-8)[Brett Favre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Favre "Brett Favre"), the team's starting quarterback, completed his 18th season with the Packers and finished in the top 10 of most season passing statistics.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-11) He was complemented by a defense that gave up the sixth least amount of points during the season.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-12) The Packers received a bye week in the Wild Card round before hosting the [Seattle Seahawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Seahawks "Seattle Seahawks") in the Divisional round.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-13) The Packers blew out the Seahawks 42–20 in what became known as the [Snow Globe Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_Globe_Game "Snow Globe Game").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-14) With their higher seeding, the Packers were scheduled to host the Giants at [Lambeau Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeau_Field "Lambeau Field") on January 20, 2008, for the NFC Championship Game. The _[Green Bay Press-Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green\_Bay\_Press-Gazette "Green Bay Press-Gazette")_ predicted cold weather for the game, with the [wind chill factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_chill_factor "Wind chill factor") bringing the daily low down to −22°F (−30°C); the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") issued a wind chill advisory prior to the start of the game.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-15) The Packers were 7.5 point favorites.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-16)

The Packers started the game with possession, although they were forced to punt after reaching mid-field. The Giants then proceeded to drive the length of the field, going 71 yards in 14 plays, before the Packers stopped them on the 11-yard line. The Giants attempted a field goal, which was converted by [Lawrence Tynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Tynes "Lawrence Tynes") for a 3–0 lead. The next three drives, two by the Packers and one by the Giants, ended in punts. The Giants gained possession at mid-field after the last Packers punt and again drove into field goal range. The Packers again stopped the Giants on third down, forcing another field goal attempt. Tynes made a 37-yard field goal to increase the Giants' lead to 6–0. On the first play of the ensuing drive, Brett Favre completed a 90-yard touchdown pass to [Donald Driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Driver "Donald Driver"), giving the Packers a 7–6 lead. The next three drives ended in punts, with the Packers regaining possession at mid-field. After a short drive, [Mason Crosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_Crosby "Mason Crosby") converted a 36-yard field goal, bringing the score to 10–6. With just over a minute left in the half, the Giants drove 40 yards but a sack on fourth down forced a [turnover on downs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnover_on_downs "Turnover on downs"). The Packers ran one play before halftime.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-ESPNPLAY-17)

The Giants started the second half with the ball and engineered a 12-play, 68-yard drive that culminated in a one-yard rushing touchdown by Brandon Jacobs; the touchdown gave the Giants the lead again, 13–10. After a long return on the kick-off by [Tramon Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tramon_Williams "Tramon Williams"), the Packers started with a short field. The Packers scored six plays later on a 12-yard touchdown pass from Favre to [Donald Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Lee_(American_football) "Donald Lee (American football)"). With the extra point, the Packers took the lead back, 17–13. On the next drive, the Giants started near mid-field and drove for a touchdown, another rushing score, this time by [Ahmad Bradshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Bradshaw "Ahmad Bradshaw"), to bring the score to 20–17. The Packers tied the game on the next drive with a 37-yard field goal by Crosby. The Packers had two more drives before the end of the game, both of which ended in three-and-outs. The Giants remaining three possessions ended in a punt and two missed field goals, including a 36-yard attempt as time expired in the fourth quarter.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-ESPNPLAY-17)

The Packers won the coin toss before overtime and chose to receive the ball first.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-TITLE1-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-TITLE2-19) On the second play of the drive, after a short rush, Favre threw a pass intended for Driver but was intercepted by [Corey Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corey_Webster "Corey Webster"). On the ensuing drive, the Giants only gained five yards, setting up a 47-yard field goal attempt. Tynes converted the attempt to give the Giants the victory, 23–20.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-ESPNPLAY-17)

| Game information |
| --- |

Post-game analysis focused on the competitive nature of the game, the impacts of the weather, individual performances, and the question of Favre's future. The _[Green Bay Press-Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green\_Bay\_Press-Gazette "Green Bay Press-Gazette")_ commented that it appeared neither team truly wanted to win, with each giving the other multiple opportunities to secure a victory.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-CHANCES-23) However, in the end, with the game going to overtime, being won on a walk-off field goal, the cold weather, and Favre's legacy in the balance, the newspaper noted that it would be a game to remember for many years.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-CHALLENGE-24)

The weather ended up making the game the second coldest in Lambeau Field history up to that point, with temperatures dropping from −1°F (−18°C) at kick-off to −3°F (−19°C) by the end of the game (the wind chill dropped as low as −24°F (−31°C) by the end of the game).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-CHALLENGE-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-INSIDER-25) The weather was so cold, that Giants' head coach [Tom Coughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Coughlin "Tom Coughlin")'s face became bright red during the game, creating a lasting image that represented the challenging conditions that players and personnel faced on the field.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-COUGH-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-ORAL-27) Sports commentators noted that the weather conditions also likely impacted the game, including on the late missed field goals by Lawrence Tynes.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-COUGH-26)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-TYNES-28)

Regarding Favre's future, the Packers quarterback had just completed one of his most productive seasons of his career, finishing in second place in MVP voting.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-30) However, the team had drafted [Aaron Rodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Rodgers "Aaron Rodgers") in 2005 and Favre had been contemplating retirement since at least 2006.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-32) Even though his teammates stated their belief he would return, the way the game ended, with Favre throwing an interception (similar to the end of the [4th and 26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_and_26 "4th and 26") playoff game against the [Philadelphia Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Eagles "Philadelphia Eagles")) strengthened the belief that he would not commit to another season and retire.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-PLAYOFF-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-34) Favre noted after the game that his decision would be made quickly, after talking with the Packers coaches.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-FAVRE-35)

[Plaxico Burress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaxico_Burress "Plaxico Burress") led the offensive output for the Giants with 11 catches for 151 yards; both figures tied or set playoff records for players against the Packers.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-BURRESS-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-OFFENSE-37) Brandon Jacobs and Ahmad Bradshaw combined for a strong running game, gaining 130 yards on the ground and two touchdowns.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-SCORE-22) This contrasted strongly with the Packers run game, with Ryan Grant only gaining 29 yards on 13 rushes for the whole game.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-CHALLENGE-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-INSIDER-25) The lack of a running game forced the Packers to be one-dimensional and rely on the passing game.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-TITLE1-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-TITLE2-19) The offense then fell apart in the second half, with the Packers having one of their worst playoff halves in history.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-OFFENSE-37)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-CHANCES-23) Sports commentators noted that Favre appeared to be pressing his performance, trying to do too much and force throws to his receivers. His final performance was surprising, considering his past success at Lambeau Field in cold weather games.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-FLAT-38)

Individual plays and players were highlighted during the post-game analysis. Favre's 90-yard touchdown pass to Donald Driver, which was the longest in Packers' playoff history at that time, was identified as a key play of the game, while Favre's interception in overtime was a crucial mistake.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-FUMBLE-39)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-INSIDER-25) Favre noted that the interception came about because he did not throw the ball wide enough, which gave the defense an opportunity to catch the ball.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-PLAYOFF-33) Tynes' multiple misses in the fourth quarter could have been huge momentum swings, however the Packers were unable to capitalize on these mistakes.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-FLAT-38) Tynes was also highlighted for coming through in the end and not letting his earlier misses phase him.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-TYNES-28) Two fumbles also were costly, for different reasons. First, Favre was intercepted in the fourth quarter, although [R. W. McQuarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._W._McQuarters "R. W. McQuarters") fumbled the ball on the return and the Packers recovered it. Second, on a punt return, the Giants fumbled the ball and [Jarrett Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarrett_Bush "Jarrett Bush") tried to pick the ball up instead of falling on it and missed, allowing the [Domenik Hixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenik_Hixon "Domenik Hixon") to recover it and retain possession for the Giants.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-FUMBLE-39) Other than the beginning of the second half, the Packers defense performed well, with [Tramon Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tramon_Williams "Tramon Williams"), [A. J. Hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._J._Hawk "A. J. Hawk"), [Atari Bigby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari_Bigby "Atari Bigby") all noted for their performance.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-CHALLENGE-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-CHANCES-23)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-FUMBLE-39)

After their victory, the Giants moved on to [Super Bowl XLII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLII "Super Bowl XLII"), where they faced the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots"). The Patriots, under [Tom Brady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Brady "Tom Brady"), had completed a perfect 16–0, the first time an NFL team had a perfect regular season record under a 16-game season.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-40) The Patriots also won two playoff games to advance to the Super Bowl, meaning that they were attempting to become the first NFL team to win every regular and postseason game in a season since the [1972 Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Miami_Dolphins_season "1972 Miami Dolphins season").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-41) The teams played a competitive game; after the Patriots took the lead late in the game, the Giants drove down the field and scored. Their drive was aided by the famous [Helmet Catch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmet_Catch "Helmet Catch"), which helped the Giants secure a 17–14 victory and the NFL Championship.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-42)

After the season, Favre announced his retirement. Just a few months later, Favre rescinded his retirement and publicly stated his desire to return to the Packers for the [2008 NFL season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NFL_season "2008 NFL season"). The Packers publicly committed to [Aaron Rodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Rodgers "Aaron Rodgers") as Favre's successor. After much discussion, Favre agreed to a trade to the [New York Jets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Jets "New York Jets") and Rodgers was reaffirmed as the starter for the Packers in 2008.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-43) Rodgers led the Packers to the playoffs in the 2009 season and then won [Super Bowl XLV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLV "Super Bowl XLV") in the 2010 season.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-EVT-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-45)

The game has been characterized by multiple sports commentators as one of the greatest championship games in league history.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-47) In 2019, the league identified the game as the 54th greatest game from the first 100 years of the history of the NFL.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-48) It also became an important part of the [Giants–Packers rivalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giants%E2%80%93Packers_rivalry "Giants–Packers rivalry"), which had included five championship games before this one.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-49) It has been remembered for its cold weather, with Giants' coach [Tom Coughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Coughlin "Tom Coughlin")'s red face becoming an indelible image from the game.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-ORAL-27)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-COUGH-26) The weather also impacted the play on the field and made Tynes' game-winning field goal even more improbable and memorable. With Favre's retirement and then trade to the Jets after the season, the NFC Championship became the last game Favre would play in his career with the Packers and ensured that his last pass as a Packer was an interception.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-FROZE-50) The game was representative of Favre's playoff failures in the 2000s, where he lost six games and threw more interceptions than touchdowns.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-51) For [Eli Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Manning "Eli Manning"), the victory against the Packers and then the Patriots in the Super Bowl helped establish his quarterback credentials.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_NFC_Championship_Game#cite_note-52)

5.title: Ice Picked: Favre's interception in OT leads to Giant upset
5.description: When Green Bay won the coin flip in overtime of the NFC Championship Game against the New York Giants, the stage was set for Brett Favre to ride off in a blaze of glory to his Super Bowl matchup for the ages against Tom Brady and the Patriots. But, on second and 8, Favre made a fatal mistake. No one knew at the time it would be Favre's last pass with the Packers.
5.content:
Jan. 21, 2008

**Green Bay** -The Green Bay Packers, a franchise that had never lost a playoff at home in their first eight decades of existence, have now been toppled three times in the last six years.

Following in the footsteps of Atlanta in 2002 and Minnesota in 2004 at the wild-card level, the New York Giants stormed into icy Lambeau Field on Sunday night like they owned the place and whipped the Packers, 23-20, in the NFC Championship Game.

Lawrence Tynes, a kicker who did not have a single pressurized field-goal attempt in the first 18 games, drilled one from 47 yards 2 minutes 35 seconds into overtime. It sent the Giants (13-6) into Super Bowl XLII against the New England Patriots (18-0) on Feb. 3 and the Packers home.

"All the plans and the hopes we had are out the window," general manager Ted Thompson said. "It's a shame. I certainly didn't think we played our best, and the Giants played very well."

A 7½-point favorite, the Packers (14-4) were beaten on both sides of the ball just as they were as a 6½-point favorite against both the Falcons in '02 (a 27-7 defeat) and against the Vikings in '04 (a 31-17 loss).

"You're devastated," defensive tackle Ryan Pickett said. "Somebody celebrating on your field. We thought we were the better team."

As it turned out, the Giants proved conclusively that they were the better team. They were the more physical team for 60 minutes, although after a passive start the Packers did respond in the middle stages of the game and led on three occasions.

However, the Packers were outgained on the ground, 134 yards to 28, the most telling indicator of how one-sided the flow of the game really was. The Giants also had a 17½-minute edge in time of possession.

"We put ourselves in position and had home field in the NFC Championship Game," coach Mike McCarthy said. "But we didn't finish the race. It's a tough lesson to learn, especially in front of our home crowd."

It was the Packers' worst upset loss since Super Bowl XXXII, when they were favored by 11½ points against Denver.

By winning, the Giants joined the New England Patriots of 1985 and the Pittsburgh Steelers of 2005 as the only teams to reach the Super Bowl after three straight road victories. The fifth-seeded Giants are the most surprising NFC champion since coach Ray Malavasi's Los Angeles Rams of 1979 advanced with a 9-7 regular-season record.

The hurt was palpable in the quiet locker room afterward. After unexpectedly gaining another home game when the Giants stunned top-seeded Dallas last week, there was a segment of the team's fan base that figured all the club had to do was show up and the Giants would fold.

In fact, it was the Packers who folded, defensively in the third quarter and offensively for most of the game.

"I'm not going to say I thought we had this one but I felt like everything had fallen into place," Brett Favre said. "All that was left was to play the game."

The Giants grew stronger and stronger as the frigid evening unfolded. If not for missed field-goal attempts of 43 and 36 yards by Tynes in the final 7 minutes, the Packers wouldn't even have gotten to overtime.

Tynes' second miss, after a high snap with 4 seconds left, brought the extra session. When Green Bay won the coin flip, the stage was set for the 38-year-old Favre to ride off in a blaze of glory to his Super Bowl matchup for the ages against Tom Brady.

But, on second and 8, Favre made a fatal mistake, the type that has marred the second half of his illustrious career in playoff losses against San Francisco in 1998 (79.7 passer rating), St. Louis in '01 (53.5), Atlanta in '02 (54.4), Philadelphia in '03 (82.4) and Minnesota in '04 (55.4). His passer rating was 70.7 in this one, behind Eli Manning's 72.3.

Favre took a deep drop against a blitz, which was picked up well. He then fired a deep sideline pattern to Donald Driver, who was working against cornerback Corey Webster.

However, the pass didn't have much on it and it was underthrown. Webster intercepted, returning it 9 yards to the Green Bay 34. Tynes followed with his decisive kick three plays later.

"I just didn't throw it outside enough," Favre said. "If I throw it out where I would have liked to. . . . It was a shake route. Donald ran it more like an out, which was fine. It just didn't get out far enough. It's too bad."

Thus, the Giants claimed their 10th straight victory on the road.

"The real, real key is the heart of this team," said Giants coach Tom Coughlin, a Packers assistant in 1986 and '87. "The heart is definitely in the right place. And they are a team."

On offense, the Giants established immediately that they would not be intimidated by the weather (minus-1 degree with minus-23 wind chill index at kickoff), a record crowd of 72,740 and a Green Bay team that was well-rested and with fewer injuries.

Manning directed a 14-play, 71-yard drive for an opening field goal in which the much-maligned quarterback established that towering Plaxico Burress could get open basically whenever he wanted to against overmatched Al Harris.

Later, the Giants unleashed their highly effective 1-2 running punch of Brandon Jacobs and Ahmad Bradshaw, who combined for 130 yards in 37 carries.

On defense, coordinator Steve Spagnuolo did a masterful job. He turned the Packers' ground game led by Ryan Grant into mush with a front seven that steadfastly was disciplined on the back side and immovable at the point of attack.

That put the onus on Favre, which might have been sufficient because his offensive line afforded very good pass protection against the Giants' collection of three dynamic defensive ends. But other than a 90-yard touchdown pass to Donald Driver, the Packers failed to gain more than 20 yards on another play.

Green Bay finished an unsightly 1 for 10 on third down after ranking eighth during the regular season.

"We weren't in tune with the passing game like we usually are," McCarthy said.

Vulnerable at cornerback with aging R.W. McQuarters and Sam Madison, the Giants were able to avoid anything deep other than Driver's bomb behind Webster. An offensive performance that started out beautifully with two completions for 23 yards off bootlegs in the end was little better than inept.

The Packers never really sustained a drive all night.

Their field goal before the end of the half finished a 29-yard excursion that ended in disappointment when guard Jason Spitz missed linebacker Antonio Pierce on a promising third-down screen pass to Brandon Jackson.

Their third-quarter touchdown drive of 39 yards was set up by Tramon Williams' 49-yard kickoff return.

And their fourth-quarter field goal came after Mark Tauscher hopped on a fumble by McQuarters at the New York 22 after he had intercepted an ill-advised bomb from Favre.

And so, it's over. One of the most satisfying seasons in the franchise's 87-year history will not include the Super Bowl.

"We're shocked we didn't win," offensive coordinator Joe Philbin said. "When you're this close and have this type of opportunity, it hurts pretty bad."

2008 in review: NFL.
====================

by[Jon Lewis](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/author/paulsensmw/)

In 2008, the titan of television dominated in the ratings once again.

Propelled by some of the biggest draws in the sport, ratings hit ten year highs during the NFL Playoffs. On the AFC side, the New England Patriots entered the playoffs undefeated and on the heels of a regular season where they attracted massive audiences almost every week. The NFC playoff picture involved three of the most storied franchises in all of football — the New York Giants, Dallas Cowboys and Green Bay Packers. The playoffs were seemingly made for TV.

The Giants meeting against the Cowboys in the Divisional Round [drew over 40 million viewers](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2008/01/giantscowboys-draws-40-million.html), the best for a Divisional Round game since 1997. The Patriots’ Divisional Round game against the Jaguars [drew 30 million viewers](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2008/01/ratings-game.html), the most viewed Saturday night program on CBS since the 1994 Winter Olympics. The Divisional Round as a whole [averaged 32.6 million viewers](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2008/01/idle-notes_18.html), the best since 1996. The NFC Championship Game, between the Giants and Packers, [drew 53.9 million viewers](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2008/01/over-50-million-watch-giantspackers.html) — the most for any non-Super Bowl television program since the series finale of Seinfeld ten years earlier.

And the best was yet to come. Super Bowl XLII arrived on the heels of two weeks of hype surrounding the undefeated Patriots. That alone figured to pique curiousity surrounding a game that needed no added draw. The underdog Giants had already given the Patriots a scare weeks earlier; their meeting in Week 17 of the 2007 season clinched an undefeated regular season for the Patriots, and [drew 34.5 million viewers](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2007/12/massive-audience-for-patsgiants.html) across three different networks — the most for a regular season game since 1995.

With that in mind, expectations for the Super Bowl reached almost absurd levels. There was [talk of a 50 rating and over 100 million viewers](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2008/02/giantspats-could-draw-massive-numbers.html). Even though the Giants’ upset victory over the Patriots did not reach those lofty levels, the game still ended up as the second-most viewed television program in history.

Super Bowl XLII [drew 97.5 million viewers](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2008/02/giantspats-most-watched-super-bowl-ever.html), the most ever for the Super Bowl. The game was the second-most viewed program ever, behind only the series finale of M*A*S*H in 1983, which drew 106 million.

The good times would not roll throughout the rest of the year. While ratings generally held up compared to last year, the NFL began feeling the effects of the economic downturn.

In December, the league announced that it would lay off 10% of its headquarters staff, [equaling 150 jobs](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2008/12/nfl-lays-off-150.html). For the fiscal year, the NFL expects to fall “[at least $50 million short of projected revenue](http://www.sportsbusinessjournal.com/article/60853).” Even the Super Bowl is not immune. NBC has had a more difficult time selling ads during the Super Bowl than FOX did a year earlier. Several former Super Bowl advertisers are “[‘sitting out’ the country’s premiere sports event](http://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article.cfm?articleid=2109)“, including General Motors — one of the big three U.S. automakers facing financial peril.

In other ominous news, the NFL and the NFLPA may be heading towards a confrontation in the future. In May, NFL owners [opted out of the Collective Bargaining Agreement](http://www.nfl.com/news/story?id=09000d5d80868b78&template=without-video&confirm=true), meaning the current CBA will expire after the 2010 season. With NFLPA head Gene Upshaw‘s death in August, there is a chance that “[little negotiating will get done in ’09 until the new union chief gets his (or her) feet settled](http://www.sportsbusinessdaily.com/article/126319).”

But all of that is in the future. All in all, 2008 was another strong year for the strongest of pro sports. The NFL figures to take a few hits in 2009, but nothing severe. While the 2009 playoffs figure to drop in the ratings, thanks to the absence of the Cowboys, Packers and Patriots, the league will likely continue drawing massive audiences. And though the economic crisis has had, and will continue to have an effect on the league, the NFL should be able to weather the storm more easily than its competitors.

AP Story: Giants Beat Packers 23-20 In Overtime
===============================================

Giants kicker Lawrence Tynes missed two fourth-quarter field goals, including a potential game-winning 36-yarder as regulation expired. He redeemed himself in overtime, connecting from 47 yards, ending the Packers’ season and sending the Giants to Arizona to face New England in Super Bowl XLII. - More Packers-Giants Game Center
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 Jan 19, 2008 at 06:00 PM

*   [](https://www.packers.com/news/ap-story-giants-beat-packers-23-20-in-overtime-2424075 "Share on Facebook")
*   [](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=AP+Story%3a+Giants+Beat+Packers+23-20+In+Overtime&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.packers.com%2Fnews%2Fap-story-giants-beat-packers-23-20-in-overtime-2424075 "Share on Twitter")

![Image 3: 080120driver215.jpg](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/f_auto/packers/ymqwbahpohp1jajlizac.jpg)

Eli Manning has arrived, just in time to take his [New York Giants](http://www.giants.com/) on an improbable trip to the Super Bowl. A suddenly matured Manning guided the Giants to their 10th straight road win Sunday, a frostbitten 23-20 overtime victory over the Green Bay Packers for the NFC championship.

Now comes Mission Impossible for Manning and the Giants, who will play the unbeaten [New England Patriots](http://www.patriots.com/) in two weeks for the NFL title.

After Lawrence Tynes missed a 36-yard field goal at the end of regulation following a bad snap, he got a reprieve in overtime following Corey Webster's interception of a struggling Brett Favre. He nailed a 47-yarder on his third attempt to win it, then sprinted directly to the locker room as the rest of his frozen teammates celebrated on the field.

"I screwed it up twice,'' Tynes said. "Thank God we got another opportunity.''

The Giants grabbed their first NFC championship in seven years, capping a monthlong surge that reversed a trend of mediocrity built around Manning's inconsistency. He has been a revelation in the playoffs, however, and his calm leadership keyed New York's turnaround.

Manning shook off below-zero temperatures and a wind chill that would make a Siberian husky shiver. He repeatedly put the Giants (13-6) in position to win in the third-coldest championship game ever _ and certainly the most frigid of his young career.

And then he saw Tynes make his first game-winning field goal of the season in the first OT title game in nine years.

It was the second NFC title game to go to overtime. Atlanta beat Minnesota 30-27 in 1999.

One year after older brother Peyton finally won a Super Bowl, earning MVP honors to boot, here comes Eli.

Just a month ago, Eli's moxie was being questioned as the Giants struggled to clinch a wild-card berth. He responded with the best work of his four-year career, including four touchdown passes in the season finale against the Patriots.

He and the Giants are getting another shot at New England, the first team to go 18-0. The Patriots will be after their fourth Super Bowl title in seven years on Feb. 3 at Glendale, Ariz., as well as the first completely perfect season since Miami went 17-0 in 1972.

But don't discount New York, which led the Patriots by 12 points in the third quarter before falling 38-35 on Dec. 29.

The Giants have won at Tampa and Dallas since, and now at Lambeau Field, where they shut down Brett Favre nearly all game.

Favre, seeking a return to the Super Bowl after a decade's absence, struggled in the minus-3 degree temperature and wind-chills that reached minus-24. He wound up 19-for-35 for 236 yards and two interceptions. The second, by Corey Webster in overtime, set up Tynes' winner.

When Tynes missed a 43-yard field goal with 6:49 remaining, it was just a temporary setback. And when he flopped on the kick that ended regulation, Tynes could only ask for one more try.

Webster gave it to him, and he sent the Giants into the Super Bowl.

New York was aided greatly by four penalties against the Packers during the Giants' seven-minute, 69-yard march to begin the second half. Brandon Jacobs bolted in from about an inch out after successive offside calls just moments after his third-down fumble was recovered by tight end Kevin Boss. But the biggest miscue was Nick Collins' 15-yard roughing-the-passer penalty on Manning, whose throw was blocked on a third-down play.

Jacobs faked a Lambeau Leap after his score, incensing the hardy souls in the full house of 72,470.

They were stamping their frozen feet in delight seconds later when Tramon Williams, seemingly trapped along the left sideline, cut right and returned the kickoff 49 yards to the New York 39. Then it was the Giants' turn to commit a costly, senseless penalty when Sam Madison negated a third-down stop with a personal foul against Vernand Morency.

{sportsad300}Favre immediately pounced with a brilliant play-fake that sprung tight end Donald Lee free in the back of the end zone for a 12-yard TD reception and a 17-13 lead.

With the footing holding on a field heated by pipes underneath, Domenik Hixon got the Giants' next scoring drive started with a 33-yard kickoff runback. Then, Manning kept picking apart the Packers' staple man coverage, a 23-yard diving catch by Amani Toomer setting up rookie Ahmad Bradshaw's 4-yard TD run.

Rookie Mason Crosby's 37-yard field goal tied it 20-20 after a huge break for the Packers. Favre's desperation heave was intercepted by R.W. McQuarters deep in New York territory, but he fumbled when he was hit by Grant on his return. Tackle Mark Tauscher recovered, giving the Packers another life.

Manning was, well, cool on New York's first series, driving the Giants 71 yards on 14 plays, going 5-for-8 for 55 yards before Tynes kicked a 29-yarder.

Green Bay went backward on its next series, an ugly three-and-out on which Favre passed three times, all behind the line of scrimmage. Total yardage: minus-3 yards.

Just as unseemly was 20-year veteran punter Jeff Feagles' first kick in a championship game on New York's next possession, a 21-yard shank.

After Tynes nailed a 37-yarder for a 6-0 lead, Koren Robinson had Packers fans holding their breath as he overran the kickoff, then bobbled it before recovering at the Green Bay 10.

Then Favre and Donald Driver took their breath away with the longest pass in team playoff history.

The cagey veteran receiver shook off a bump by Webster to break free as Favre double-pumped. Driver caught the ball at the 29 and raced the final 71 yards being chased by three Giants. None came close to preventing Driver's first touchdown in four months.

Favre extended his NFL record with his 18th straight postseason game with a TD pass. Few have been so spectacular.

Crosby added a 36-yard field goal with 1:30 left in the half for a 10-6 lead. But Burress snatched the ball from Al Harris for a 32-yard completion, then dropped a long pass near the Green Bay end zone.

Most players from both teams sprinted to the locker rooms at halftime the way Driver sped away from defenders on his touchdown.
